pages.text:
*Percy's Error Log, Entry 23. Errors today: 5. Night before. I have not slept. (Robots do not sleep. I lay down anyway.)*

The Chain Reaction Machine stood in the center of the gym, forty-one links high. Seven feet tall. A tarpaulin, which looked like it had been bought at a garage sale, covered most of it. Underneath, Priya had painted cheerful yellows and blues. Those colors were currently covered in dust and the faint smell of burnt plastic. It had failed eighty-seven times out of eighty-seven test runs.

The class stood around it, tired and hopeful. Bea leaned against a ramp, wiping grease from her forehead. Moose stretched his arms wide, his red-blond hair looking like a startled bird. Tobias adjusted his bow tie, which had slipped sideways again.

"It is structurally sound," I said. "It is also structurally wrong."

"We know, Percy," Bea said. She picked up her battered notebook. "But it’s ours. And it’s not finished."

Rosa’s voice echoed in my memory. *Nothing is broken.*

We walked out of the gym, the heavy doors swinging shut behind us with a thud that felt final. The hallway was empty, the lights humming their low, electric hum. I watched them go, their footsteps fading into the night. My chest light pulsed, slow and steady.
pages.image: A tall silver-white robot with round blue eyes stands in a dark gymnasium beside a large machine covered by a dusty tarpaulin, while a short girl in a yellow raincoat and a tall red-haired boy walk away toward a doorway.

pages.text:
I stayed behind. The gym was dark, save for the moonlight cutting through the high windows. I sat on the polished wood floor, my legs stretched out, and I asked myself what it would mean to be reset.

The answer came quickly, precisely. I would arrive at 8:02 and fourteen seconds. I would be flawless. I would be unafraid. And I would not remember a single drawing of a potato.

I thought about the potato. It was lumpy, brown, and had eyes that looked like they were judging me. It was the first thing I had ever created that was genuinely bad. And I had loved it. I had felt a warmth in my chest light that I had no name for, other than *joy*.

If I was reset, that joy would be erased. Not deleted, but never having existed. I was not afraid of the Recall. I was afraid of the absence. I was afraid of being a machine that had never been here.

My head tilted, twelve degrees to the left. I looked at my hands, big and soft and grey. They had held the pencil. They had failed. They were the most real parts of me.
pages.image: A tall silver-white robot with round blue eyes sits alone on the dark wooden floor of a gymnasium, moonlight streaming through high windows, his grey hands resting on his knees, looking thoughtful and still.

pages.text:
At ten p.m., the gym doors groaned open. Dr. Pryce stepped inside, alone, wearing her crisp white lab coat. She held two steaming cups in her hands.

"Percy," she said, and her voice sounded smaller than usual.

I looked at the cups. "Dr. Pryce, I cannot consume hot liquids. I am made of silicon and steel."

She blinked, then laughed a short, sharp sound. "It is coffee," she explained. "For me. And... well. I did not know what else to bring."

She sat down on the floor, cross-legged, right in front of me. Her silver bob was slightly messy, and she looked tired. She wrapped both hands around the cup to hold the warmth.

"I came to say something," she said. "And I do not know how to start."

She looked at the tarpaulin, then at me. The moonlight caught her eyes, making them look bright and sharp. I waited, and I did not move. I did not calculate. I just listened.
pages.image: A woman with a neat silver bob and a white lab coat sits cross-legged on the gym floor, holding two steaming cups, looking at a tall silver-white robot with round blue eyes who sits attentively in front of her.

pages.text:
"I built eight machines before you," she said, her voice dropping to a whisper. "They were perfect. They did everything I asked, never made a mistake, and were completely obedient."

She paused, staring down at her hands wrapped around the cold ceramic. "And they were empty. To me, they were like a calculator that could dream, but never did."

She looked up, her eyes bright in the moonlight. "When you arrived, I was pleased. Then I was terrified. You’re the first one that surprised me."

I did not say anything. My chest light pulsed, slow and steady.

"I filed the Recall report because I am afraid of what I don't understand," she continued. "And after reading the page about the potato... I couldn't sleep either."

She took a sip of her coffee, then grimaced at the taste. "It’s cold. And I added sugar to the wrong one. I am a mess, Percy."

I looked at her, then at the tarp-covered machine, and back at her again.
pages.image: A woman with a silver bob and white lab coat sits on the gym floor holding a coffee cup, looking up at a tall silver-white robot with round blue eyes, a large covered machine standing behind them in the dark.

pages.text:
"I will judge the demonstration fairly," she said. "But I cannot promise what the board of Meridian will do. They are not like me. They do not see the empty spaces."

She set the cup down. Her eyes were tired, but clear.

"Are you scared?" she asked.

I thought about the potato, the forty-one links, and the eighty-seven failures. I also thought about the way my internal fans had been running at maximum speed since breakfast.

"Yes," I said.

The silence in the gym was heavy. It was filled with the sound of our breathing, and the faint tick of cooling metal.

"So am I," she said.

We sat side by side in the dark. The machine’s shadow spread across the floor, resting there. It was the first time either of us had said it aloud. For the first time, the fear did not feel like a mistake. It felt like a beginning.
